meta.descriptionEn: On the night of November 22, 1987, a normal Sunday evening in Chicago turned strange. During a sports segment, a figure in a Max Headroom mask suddenly replaced the news on WGN-TV. Two hours later, it happened again on PBS station WTTW in the middle of a Doctor Who episode, this time with sound, bizarre rants and a baffling finale. Thousands of viewers saw it. Engineers could not stop the second one. The FCC investigated, yet no one was ever identified. How was it done? Who had the skill and the equipment? Was it an inside job, or Chicago's underground hackers? Follow the evidence, the theories and the mystery that has lasted decades.
meta.descriptionUr: 22 November 1987 ki raat Chicago mein ek aam Sunday achanak ajeeb ho gayi. WGN-TV ki khabron ke dauran Max Headroom ka mask pehne ek shakhs screen par aa gaya. articleEn: It was the night of 22 November 1987, a Sunday evening in Chicago. People were sitting in their homes watching television, and everything seemed perfectly normal. At 9:14 p.m., WGN-TV's Nine O'Clock News was in the middle of its sports segment. Suddenly the screen went black. For about 15 seconds nothing appeared.

Then a strange figure came into view, wearing a Max Headroom mask and sunglasses. He swayed awkwardly in front of a metal panel. There was no voice, only a sharp buzz. About two hours later, around 11:20 p.m., it happened again. This time the target was PBS station WTTW, which was airing an episode of Doctor Who called Horror of Fang Rock. This time there was sound, and the video ran longer. The whole interruption lasted about 90 seconds. At the end, a woman appeared holding a flyswatter, and then the mysterious broadcast abruptly ended.

The questions are simple. Who were these people? How did they take over the signals of two major stations? And why have they never been caught? The FCC investigated, but those responsible were never identified, and the mystery remains unsolved decades later. In this article we look at who Max Headroom was, the story of each station, how the stunt was technically possible, and what the theories say.

articleEn: So who was Max Headroom? He was not a real person but a fictional character played by actor Matt Frewer. He was presented as the first computer-generated TV presenter, and he was known for his sharp wit, arrogant manner, stuttering voice and constantly shifting pitch. The character was created by British video directors and artists George Stone, Annabel Jankel and Rocky Morton.

Max was billed as computer-generated, and some people even believed it. In reality, Frewer sat in front of a blue screen wearing prosthetic makeup, contact lenses and a plastic suit. Bright lighting and editing effects strengthened the illusion, so viewers really thought it was CGI. He debuted in April 1985 on Britain's Channel 4 in a cyberpunk TV movie called Max Headroom: 20 Minutes into the Future.

In the story, a journalist named Edison Carter flees his enemies into a parking garage, and his motorcycle crashes into an entry barrier. The barrier carried the sign "Max. headroom 2.3 metres," a common UK sign giving vehicle height limits, and the character took his name from it. Carter was unconscious, and an AI program based on his mind was created. It became a TV host who lived only inside broadcast signals and computer systems. Interestingly, early episodes of The Max Headroom Show began with static, as if Max himself were hijacking the broadcast signal. On the show Max introduced music videos, commented on various topics, and later interviewed guests in front of a live audience.

The show was an instant hit in the UK. In its second and third years it was also shown on the US cable channel Cinemax. Max took over advertising too, becoming the global spokesperson for New Coke, with the famous line "Catch the wave!" Then in 1987 an American drama series called Max Headroom aired on ABC, in which Frewer played both Max and Carter, who worked together as allies. It ran for only two seasons, from 1987 to 1988.

Max's look came down to three things: a shiny dark suit, sunglasses, and a geometric background that moved behind him. Keep those three in mind. Now imagine someone building that same mask, those sunglasses and that background, and breaking into someone else's broadcast. What would happen?

articleEn: Now to Chicago, where on the night of 22 November 1987 the signals of two stations were disrupted. First, a look at the stations. The first was WGN-TV, channel 9. Its broadcasts began in 1948, and it was tied to the company behind the Chicago Tribune newspaper. The letters WGN stood for World's Greatest Newspaper, the Tribune's tagline. The hijacker's remarks would later mention this.

When the DuMont network shut down in 1956, WGN-TV became an independent station. It used a mix of sitcoms, films, cartoons and local news. Sports were its great strength. Broadcasts of Chicago Cubs baseball and other teams made it a strong alternative to the city's three network stations. On 9 November 1978, WGN-TV became the second US television station to reach cable subscribers across the country by satellite. This was called a superstation. After that, Cubs baseball, Bulls basketball and programs like The Bozo Show became very popular across the central US.

In the 1980s WGN's ratings kept improving, and by the end of the decade it was the city's highest-rated independent station. articleEn: At 9:14 p.m., WGN-TV was airing The Nine O'Clock News, and the sports segment had begun. Dan Roan was presenting highlights of that afternoon's Bears-Lions game, and viewers were watching closely. Then the screen suddenly went black. People at home probably thought their televisions had broken. According to sources, the black screen lasted about 15 seconds.

Then a picture appeared, and it was very strange. An unknown person wore a Max Headroom mask and sunglasses. He swayed erratically, and behind him was a panel of corrugated metal that was half rotating. It seemed meant to imitate Max Headroom's famous geometric background effect. As for sound, the intruders could not send any. Viewers heard only a sharp, droning buzz like static and garbled noise. Imagine thousands of Chicago homes watching sports highlights when a masked person starts swaying on screen with no explanation.

Meanwhile, WGN's engineers had to take back control, because someone else had seized their broadcast. Their solution was to change the frequency of the link connecting the studio to the transmitter, which sat atop the John Hancock Center. The move worked. The pirate feed was suppressed, and WGN's own broadcast reached viewers again.

How long did it all last? Here the sources differ slightly, and we should be honest about it. One account says the whole interruption lasted about 30 seconds. Another says about 17 seconds, and another 25 seconds, while another description mentions only 13 seconds of video. So estimates range from 13 to 30 seconds. What everyone agrees on is that the incident was very brief. Still, that short time stunned Chicago viewers.

When the broadcast returned, Dan Roan, who sources say was bemused, said, "Well, if you're wondering what happened, so am I." In a live newscast, it was hard to imagine a more honest answer. One source words it slightly differently, as "what's happened," but the meaning is the same. Roan joked further that the computer running the news seemed to have gone out of control and "took off and went wild." He then restarted the report that had been interrupted, the highlights of that day's Bears game.

On the surface the story seemed over. But this was only the first part, because about two hours later a second incident was coming that same night. This time the hijackers would have sound, and more time. So what happened at 11:20 at the second station? Let's find out.

articleEn: Now to the night's second incident. At about 11:20 p.m., Chicago's PBS station WTTW was airing the Doctor Who serial Horror of Fang Rock, the first part of the serial. Viewers were calmly watching a science fiction story when the signal was suddenly disrupted. This time the Max Headroom-like character apparently returned. The difference was that sound could be heard, though distorted.

Over the next minute or so, the masked figure spoke short, seemingly disconnected sentences, accompanied by excited noises and screams. He first said something about nerds. Then he made a nasty remark about WGN sportscaster Chuck Swirsky. After that, he raised a can of Pepsi and repeated the slogan "Catch the wave," from the Coca-Cola ad featuring the real Max Headroom. Then he sang "Your love is fading" and hummed part of the theme from the 1959 animated series Clutch Cargo.

Next he said, "I still see the X." This was a reference to the final episode of that same show, which some people mistakenly hear as "I stole CBS." He also put on a knitted glove and said it was dirty and that the other glove was with his brother. None of it connected. He also claimed to have made a great masterpiece of "Greatest World Newspaper nerds." Remember, WGN stands for World's Greatest Newspaper.

At the end came a jump cut. At the edge of the screen a woman appeared in a French maid outfit and mask, holding a flyswatter, with the character half out of frame. He held up the Max Headroom mask and screamed, "Oh no, they're coming to get me! Ah, make it stop!" At that moment the woman began hitting him with the flyswatter. Then the picture slowly dissolved into static, and viewers returned to Doctor Who. The whole interruption lasted about 90 seconds, far longer than the first.

The big question is why WTTW couldn't stop it. The reason was that no engineer was present at the Sears Tower at that hour. Station spokesman Anders Yocom said technicians "attempted to take corrective measures, but couldn't." In Yocom's words, "By the time our people began looking into what was going on, it was over." Air director Paul Rizzo recalled that "as the content got weirder, we got increasingly stressed out about our inability to do anything about it." The decision to end it was also made by the hijackers themselves.

After the broadcast ended, WTTW received a lot of phone calls. Viewers wanted to know what on earth that had been. Now the question was bigger. How were both stations' signals taken over? That is the technical secret, and we unravel it in the next section.

According to sources, the intrusion worked by sending a more powerful microwave transmission to the stations' towers. It was stronger than the signal the stations themselves were sending to their towers. That is the basis of the entire event.

The result was a capture effect. In simple terms, when two signals collide, the stronger one takes over. So viewers' televisions received the picture the hijackers sent, not the one the station was sending. That is why WGN's engineers changed the frequency. Once the link frequency between studio and transmitter changed, the pirate signal lost its effect.

How hard was it? Some experts say the stunt required a great deal of technical skill, along with a large amount of transmitting power. Not everyone has such equipment and knowledge. Experts also said the pirate broadcast most likely came from a place with line of sight to both stations' towers. And where were those towers? On two tall buildings in downtown Chicago. WGN's transmitter was on the John Hancock Center and WTTW's tower was in the Sears Tower. So the person targeting them needed a spot from which both buildings were visible, which narrows the possible locations somewhat.

One thing is worth understanding here. Two different stations were targeted in one night, so the targets do not seem accidental, though that is only our guess. There is another point. In the second incident no engineer was present at the tower, so the hijackers were able to play audio and stay on air longer. This difference clearly shows how much the presence of engineers mattered in the first incident. In one place a response was possible, in the other it was not.

Also remember that the stunt was difficult in 1987. And today? In 2009, American television stations switched from analog to digital signals. After that change, repeating this kind of act became nearly impossible. That is what the sources say. In other words, the event was tied to the technology of a particular era. Put differently, the analog world of 1987 made this opportunity possible.

So here is the summary: a stronger microwave signal, the capture effect, line of sight to both towers, and the absence of an engineer at WTTW's tower. But wait. That is only the method. The real question remains: who did it, and what was the purpose of all this effort? The Federal Communications Commission, the FCC, began investigating immediately. articleEn: The FCC launched a criminal investigation, but what was the result? Investigators could not find the people responsible for the hijacking. No one has ever claimed responsibility for the stunt. No confession came forward, and their identities remain unknown to this day. Still, people did not stay quiet. Over the years there were many unofficial inquiries, and plenty of speculation went on online. Remember that both hijackings happened on the same night, 22 November 1987, about two hours apart, and both targeted Chicago stations.

Two big theories are heard most often in these discussions. The first is that it may have been the work of an angry employee. Some people think it could have been an inside job by a disgruntled current or former WGN employee. Remember, this is only a theory. The second hijacking included some references connected to WGN. For example, the masked person criticized WGN sportscaster Chuck Swirsky by name. Then he said "Greatest World Newspaper nerds," which was a joke on WGN's call letters, which stand for World's Greatest Newspaper. But does this prove the culprit was a WGN employee? No. These are only hints, not firm proof, so treat it as guesswork.

Now the second theory. Some people believe members of Chicago's underground hacker community may be behind it. This idea gets support from the technical side. Experts say the job required extensive technical expertise and a very large amount of transmitting power. They also say the broadcast probably came from a place in line of sight of both stations' towers. Such skills and equipment were not available to everyone. That is why some think the culprit was a skilled technical person or group.

If they had been caught, what would the penalty have been? An FCC official was cited in newspapers saying the people responsible could have faced a fine of up to $100,000 and up to a year in prison. But time passed. The matter had a five-year statute of limitations, and it expired in 1992. So even if those people were identified now, they would not face criminal punishment. How strange: a penalty that was once possible has legally lapsed, yet the questions are still alive.

Look at one more aspect. The content of the second broadcast was very odd and disordered. A Pepsi can, the Clutch Cargo tune, and a flyswatter had no clear connection to one another. Perhaps that confusion was the point, or perhaps it was just a joke. We cannot say for sure. That is why the motive is still the biggest mystery. Even after the investigation, neither identity nor reason was known.

Friends, in short, the FCC's investigation came to nothing. There are two big theories, an insider or hackers, but neither has been proven. So what is the legacy of this story? What effect did it have on popular culture? And what lessons does it hold for today's world?

articleEn: The echoes of the incident soon turned up in the media. The first reference came from another Chicago station, WMAQ-TV. During sports highlights in one newscast, the station jokingly included clips of the hijacking. The sports anchor was Mark Giangreco. According to Giangreco, many people thought it was real, and the station received all sorts of calls about it. In other words, the moment was so convincing to viewers that even a joke looked real to many. This was the first sign of the incident's impact.

Then the story reached animation. In Space Ghost Coast to Coast, in the season 3 episode "Freakshow," a broadcast intruder keeps breaking into the feed. The intruder is named Commander Andy, played by Andy Merrill. He constantly disrupts Space Ghost's interviews. When Moltar tries to stop the disruption, a short clip of the Max Headroom incident appears on his monitor.

According to Motherboard, the event became an influential "cyberpunk hacking trope," a style repeated again and again in later stories and media. Eminem took on a Max-like look in his 2013 "Rap God" video. In the 2015 film Pixels, Matt Frewer also made a brief cameo. And on 29 July 2022, AMC announced a series reboot in which Matt Frewer will once again play Max.

What did we learn from this story? The first lesson is about technology. Could such a hijacking happen the same way today? According to sources, it was difficult even in 1987. But in 2009, when American television stations adopted digital signals in place of analog, repeating it became almost impossible.

The second lesson is human. On that night no engineer was present at WTTW's Sears Tower site, so the technicians could do nothing even though they wanted to. By contrast, at WGN the engineers changed the frequency of the studio-to-transmitter link and took back their signal within moments. This difference shows how important monitoring and quick response are. This conclusion is our own analysis, not part of any official report.

Finally, the biggest question. Decades later, we still do not know who was behind the mask. Sources say the identities and motives remain a mystery. So let's repeat the questions. First, who did it? An employee or hackers? These are only theories, not proven facts. Second, how did it happen? The answer is relatively clear: a stronger microwave signal created the capture effect and overpowered the stations' own signals. And third, why? What was the purpose of two short, strange broadcasts made with such effort? No one has the answer to this to this day.

In one night there were two hijackings, one mask and one flyswatter. That night of 22 November 1987 remains a mysterious chapter of Chicago television history. If you enjoyed this story, share your thoughts on who you think was behind the mask.

WGN ke engineers ne frequency badal kar signal wapas le liya. Magar yeh to sirf shuruaat thi. Do ghante baad kya hone wala tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
